abstracts.value: This dissertation presents a search for low-energy neutrinos in temporal coincidence with gravitational wave events reported by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration during the fourth observing run (O4), using 499.0 days of data collected during the liquid scintillator phase of the SNO+ experiment. The search uses inverse beta decay (IBD), which is primarily sensitive to electron antineutrinos, and neutrino-proton elastic scattering, a complementary neutral current channel providing sensitivity to all neutrino flavors. Candidate events were identified using optimized reconstruction and event-selection criteria developed with Monte Carlo simulations and validated with background-only data. The IBD background rate was measured directly from data, naturally incorporating reactor antineutrinos, geoneutrinos, radioactive backgrounds, cosmogenic backgrounds, and accidental coincidences present during detector operation. A model-independent framework was developed using flat spectrum neutrino Monte Carlo samples, allowing the detector response to be evaluated as a function of neutrino energy and applied to different theoretical emission models. As part of this work, improvements were made to the SNO+ Monte Carlo simulation, including modifications to the IBD generator to produce a true flat neutrino spectrum and corrections to the implementation of the neutrino-proton elastic scattering cross section. Detector characterization studies, including measurements of the deployed scintillator light yield and investigations of detector timing and electronics performance, were also performed to validate the detector response used throughout the analysis. The final gravitational wave-coincident dataset contained 143 candidates overlapping stable SNO+ data-taking periods. After excluding candidates classified as terrestrial or unknown by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration, the final astrophysical sample used for compact binary merger fluence limits contained 126 gravitational wave candidates. No statistically significant neutrino excess was observed in either the IBD or neutrino-proton elastic scattering channels. The IBD search observed no coincident candidates in the final astrophysical gravitational wave sample, consistent with an expected background of 1.25 ± 0.09 events. The corresponding Feldman-Cousins 90% confidence level upper limit is N90stack = 1.47 signal events. Stacked average (per gravitational wave) upper limits on the electron antineutrino fluence were derived for both monoenergetic neutrino emission and model-dependent spectra, including thermal neutrino and core-collapse supernova-inspired models used as detector sensitivity benchmarks. The neutrino-proton elastic scattering search represents the first application of this all-flavor channel to a gravitational wave-coincident neutrino search. Using an optimized ±50 s coincidence window, 108424 candidate events were observed, consistent with the expected background of 108345 ± 786 events estimated from local sidebands. The observed 0.24σ fluctuation is consistent with the background-only hypothesis. For the final astrophysical gravitational wave sample, the Feldman-Cousins method gives a 90% confidence level upper limit of N90stack = 1479.6 signal events. These results are used to derive the first all-flavor neutrino-proton elastic scattering fluence limits associated with compact binary merger candidates. The resulting SNO+ IBD fluence limits improve upon previous liquid scintillator gravitational wave-neutrino searches by approximately an order of magnitude in the few-MeV energy region, primarily due to the larger fiducial target mass, increased gravitational wave sample size, and low background rate achieved in SNO+. The neutrino-proton elastic scattering results establish the first all-flavor MeV neutrino search through this interaction channel in coincidence with gravitational wave events. Together, these analyses extend previous multi-messenger searches performed by Borexino, KamLAND, and Super-Kamiokande and demonstrate the capability of SNO+ to search for weak neutrino signals associated with astrophysical transients.

titles.title: The Search for Mev-scale Neutrinos in Temporal Coincidence With o4 Gravitational Wave Events Using the Sno+ Experiment

abstracts.value: Realistic simulation of quantum key distribution (QKD) networks requires a combination of precise models of quantum channels and network functions. Unfortunately, existing QKD network simulators lack either rigorous quantum physics modeling or network key-management and routing protocols, which limit their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose a QKD network simulator with hyperparameter tuning (QKDSim-HT), a NetSquid-based simulator specialized for polarization-based discrete-variable QKD networks. Specifically, QKDSim-HT models properties in quantum physics (photon loss, polarization-dependent depolarization, detector inefficiencies, dark counts, and dead times) as well as advanced functionalities in networking algorithms (multi-hop key relay and adaptive routing). Extensive simulations over diverse topologies reveal that the networking performance varied with respect to the fundamental properties of quantum physics, such as depolarization, fiber length, and channel attenuation. As a representative use case of QKDSim-HT, simulation results from QKDSim-HT over simple examples clearly manifest that a design of QKD networks highly affects performance of the networks. Accordingly, QKDSim-HT can serve as a practical platform for performance evaluation and optimization of quantum secured network.

titles.title: Quantum Key Distribution Network Simulator With Hyperparameter Tuning for Realistic Performance Analysis

abstracts.value: We present a unified theoretical framework for analyzing both electrostatic two-stream and electromagnetic Weibel instabilities in counterstreaming electron-positron pair plasmas. Through systematic derivation of dispersion relations in non-relativistic and relativistic regimes, we demonstrate how the symmetric mass ratio fundamentally alters instability characteristics compared to electron-ion systems. The two-stream instability, driven by longitudinal electrostatic perturbations parallel to beam motion, exhibits enhanced growth rates in pair plasmas due to equal contributions from both species, with relativistic suppression scaling as γ0−3 for both electrons and positrons. The Weibel instability, arising from transverse electromagnetic modes perpendicular to streaming directions, lacks the heavy-ion stabilization present in electron-ion plasmas, producing broader unstable spectral ranges and modified saturation levels. We derive explicit conditions determining the relative dominance of each mechanism across parameter space defined by drift velocity, wavenumber orientation, and relativistic Lorentz factor. Our analysis shows that longitudinal two-stream modes dominate at small perpendicular wavenumbers and moderate drift velocities, while transverse Weibel modes become prevalent at high perpendicular wavenumbers and large velocity spreads or temperature anisotropies. These findings have direct implications for understanding magnetic field generation, particle acceleration, and energy dissipation in astrophysical pair plasmas including pulsar wind nebulae, gamma-ray burst internal shocks, and active galactic nuclei jets where counterstreaming pair populations naturally arise.

titles.title: Suppression of two-stream and Weibel instabilities in ultra-relativistic electron–positron plasma

abstracts.value: Realistic quantum devices are open systems, and their behaviour depends not only on the subsystem of interest but also on how the environment is modelled and how the relevant observables are extracted. This thesis studies that problem in three settings. First, we study cavity-assisted qubit readout beyond the dispersive regime. We show that once coherent excitation exchange and dissipation become relevant, a microscopic treatment is needed to describe the readout quantitatively, and the optimal readout is set by a trade-off between signal accumulation and the distinguishability of the readout states. Second, we compare fermionic and spin baths in non-interacting transport models and show that spin baths reproduce fermionic reduced dynamics only in the large-bath weak-coupling limit, while clear deviations appear for smaller baths and near half-filling. Third, we study charge transport in molecular junctions using Automated Compression of Environments (ACE). There, the main difficulty is not the time evolution itself, but the extraction of the transport current, since this observable depends on system-environment correlations and is therefore not contained in the reduced system density matrix alone. We show that a probe-mode construction provides a viable route to reformulate the current as a system observable. This thesis advances our understanding of what is required for accurate modelling of open quantum dynamics across a range of solid-state settings, from cavity-assisted qubit readout to charge transport in molecular junctions.

titles.title: Developing and validating models of open quantum systems in solid-state nanostructures

abstracts.value: Using superconducting rectifiers to energize high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets is a promising approach to accelerate the uptake of HTS magnet technology. In this work, we start to address two limitations of the HTS superconducting rectifier concepts published to date; their low magnet charging voltages, and the variable properties of their HTS-based switches. Our approach is to test a centre-tapped full-wave transformer–rectifier utilizing HTS secondary windings and switch-arrays of Si <sc xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mosfet</small>s mounted on a printed-circuit board (PCB). This approach has the advantage of greatly facilitating reproducible and reliable manufacture. The rectifier demonstrated magnet charging voltages exceeding a cycle-averaged 80 mV at 100 A and with typically more than 30% of the power supplied to the primary coils delivered to the magnet. We found it to be resilient to our preliminary thermal-cycling testing, with no degradation in performance observed over eight liquid-nitrogen to ambient (77–295 K) thermal cycles. We compare the impact of voltage- and current-controlled modes for the rectifier’s power supply. Our conclusion is that superconducting rectifiers using <sc xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mosfet</small> switch arrays placed on PCBs is a very promising approach for low-current HTS magnet power supplies.

titles.title: Using Printed Circuit Boards and MOSFET Switch Arrays Toward the Reliable Manufacture of Superconducting Rectifiers

abstracts.value: Compact high turns ratio superconducting transformers are used to transfer power between low-current copper/ semiconductor-based circuits and high-current superconductor-based circuits. This type of transformer is a key component in devices, such as superconducting transformer rectifiers and superconducting current source inverters. Typically the copper winding and the superconducting winding are arranged with a turn ratio above 100:1, respectively, and are situated entirely within a cryogenic environment. The ohmic losses associated with the high count copper winding is problematic for most cryogenic applications and demands attention even when low currents on the order of 1–10 A are used. To address this problem, a transformer has been made using rare-earth barium copper oxide (REBCO) high-temperature superconductor (HTS) coated conductor for both the primary and secondary windings. The coupling coefficient and power consumption of this transformer were measured and compared to an equivalent transformer consisting of a copper primary winding and HTS secondary winding. The HTS primary was found to provide a significant reduction in transformer power consumption and a slight improvement to transformer coupling at frequencies below <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim$</tex-math></inline-formula>8 Hz. An increased transformer core loss and winding AC loss began to negate these efficiency improvements above <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim$</tex-math></inline-formula>8 Hz. In addition, cowinding the primary and secondary windings provided a higher coupling coefficient and lower power consumption for all winding combinations and frequencies tested. Finally, a short discussion on the implications of these findings respect to superconducting transformer rectifiers contextualizes the findings.

titles.title: Compact High Turns Ratio Superconducting Transformer: Comparison Between Cu and REBCO Winding Materials

abstracts.value: This article investigates the mechanical characteristics and critical current performance of aluminum-stabilized stacked REBCO tape cable (ASTC) for the circular electron-positron collider detector magnet. In-plane bending, torsion, and uniaxial tension tests are carried out, combined by finite element analysis. The correlation between critical current and strain under different loading conditions is systematically analyzed, and key mechanical thresholds are determined. Results show that the minimum allowable in-plane bending diameter is 1200 mm. The critical twist pitch is 327 mm. The critical current degrades to 95% of the initial value when the tensile strain in the REBCO tape reaches 0.37%. This study provides essential experimental data and theoretical support for the structural design and engineering application of ASTC in high-field superconducting magnets.

titles.title: Mechanical Characteristics of Aluminium-Stabilized Stacked REBCO Tape Cable for the CEPC Detector Magnet

abstracts.value: The development of large-scale superconducting quantum computers critically depends on the accurate readout of qubit states. To enable this, cryogenic parametric amplifiers have been proposed and developed, and have since found widespread use in small-signal detection applications. Among various amplifier architectures, Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) are widely adopted due to their broad bandwidth, high saturation power, and compatibility with superconducting qubits. In this work, we present a design workflow of JTWPAs based on a cosimulation approach combining electromagnetic (EM) and circuit-level simulation. We apply this method to a uniform JTWPA, comparing our simulation results with experimental data. To mitigate the challenge of constructing lumped-element circuit models usually used in the conventional simulation method, we directly perform full EM analysis of the device to accurately determine its linear response. The extracted S-parameters are then fed into a nonlinear harmonic balance simulator with Josephson junctions modeled as circuit elements. By doing so, the linear and gain properties of the JTWPA are extracted. Different factors that impact device performance including gain compression, phase matching, and fabrication imperfections are further investigated and modeled. A good agreement between simulation and measurements is identified, establishing the effectiveness of our approach in designing quantum parametric amplifiers.

titles.title: Designing Josephson Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifiers: EM-Circuit Cosimulation and Experimental Validation

abstracts.value: The q-plate is a spatially inhomogeneous SU(2) birefringent optical element that has garnered significant interest due to its ability to mediate the spin-orbit interaction of light and facilitate the generation of structured light with singularities. The q-plate features a spatially varying fast axis orientation defined by three parameters: the topological charge q, retardance delta, and the offset angle $alpha_0$. While the parameter alpha_0 can be changed many times by rotation, any change in the charge and/or retardance entails the fabrication of a new plate. This limitation can be overcome through the concept of an effective waveplate, where multiple waveplates, homogeneous or inhomogeneous, are aligned coaxially so that, under specific constraints, the composite system emulates the behavior of a single effective waveplate. This work presents a comprehensive mathematical formalism for realizing an effective waveplate through a cascaded configuration of three q-plates, each chosen as either a quarter-wave q-plate, a half-wave q-plate, or a combination thereof. Some configurations offer tunability of the retardance over the full range from 0 to $2pi$, even though q-plates with fixed retardances of $pi/2$ and pi are used in sequence to form an effective q-plate. This feature enables holonomic polarization walk on the higher-order Poincare sphere. Such a capability holds significant potential for applications involving structured light associated with the higher-order Poincare sphere, particularly in controlled polarization transformations and polarization-topology engineering.

titles.title: Mathematics of effective q-plate in polarization optics

abstracts.value: Black holes pose a lot of unsolved problems surrounding their fundamental properties. One of those puzzles is the black hole entropy problem. It has been known for a long time that black holes behave as thermodynamic systems and possess an entropy, but the question remains which microstates are responsible for this entropy. A theory of quantum gravity is needed to tackle this problem, currently the most viable example of which is string theory. The work of Strominger and Vafa, where they studied a class of asymptotically flat black holes, proves that string theory is indeed rich enough to account for the microstates responsible for the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy. Recently, the focus has shifted to asymptotically AdS black holes after the discovery of the AdS/CFT correspondence.Holographic dualities, the first example of which was discovered by Maldacena, have proven to be highly successful in providing a microstate counting for the entropy of black holes. The black hole is constructed on the gravity side of the correspondence, and the dual field theory counts its states. In this thesis we study black holes in AdS5 and their dual 4d N=1 SCFTs. The general procedure can be summarized as follows. On the field theory side, supersymmetric states are counted using the superconformal index. From the index we can obtain the entropy via a Legendre transform. By requiring that the entropy is real, we obtain a prediction for the existence of a dual black hole with that same entropy. In the dual supergravity theory we look for such solutions and compute the Euclidean on-shell action to match to the index, and the horizon area to match to the CFT entropy.This procedure was successfully applied to the minimal sector of any AdS5/CFT4 duality by Cabo-Bizet, Cassani, Martelli and Murthy, to leading order in the large N expansion. Here we aim to move beyond these results by adding flavour symmetries to the problem and by going beyond leading order at large N. On the field theory side of the duality, we study the index and entropy of flavoured SCFTs. We observe that for some theories, the simple procedure for taking the Legendre transform in the literature can no longer be applied. In all previously known examples, the index satisfies a cubic identity which leads to a simple way of deriving the entropy. We show that this identity no longer holds for certain theories but can be replaced by a sixth order identity, resulting in a different, more complicated expression for the entropy. These results suggest the existence of a new class of dual black hole solutions to match this entropy with their horizon area.We then proceed to finding these new solutions. This is a highly nontrivial problem because the dual supergravity theories contain hypermultiplet scalars. We specifically choose to work in the duality derived from M5-branes wrapping around a Riemann surface, between a family of non-Lagrangian class S SCFTs and a set of N=2 supergravities with two vector multiplets and one hypermultiplet, both parametrized by a rational number z. For z=±1, the cubic identity is satisfied and the entropy takes the familiar, simple form. Here we can easily identify the dual black holes through a relation to the five-dimensional STU model. For other values of z, we need the sixth order identity and we must include the hypermultiplet scalars in the black hole solution. To simplify the problem, we look for the near-horizon extremal geometry and restrict to two equal angular momenta. We start from the known solution for z=1 and perform an expansion around this point. We find an analytical solution to first order in the expansion. Since we only solve in the near-horizon region, we lose access to the on-shell action and chemical potentials but can still compute the charges and the entropy. The entropy through the area law matches precisely with the field theory prediction. We therefore prove that these partial solutions are the first step towards identifying the new class of black hole solutions with non-zero hypermultiplet scalars.In the final part of this thesis we move beyond the leading order at large N and add higher-derivative corrections. We focus on the universal case where only the R-symmetry is turned on. In this case, the higher-derivative action including four derivatives can be fully determined up to two constants, which can be related to the conformal anomalies of the dual field theory using the holographic map. We then set out to confirm the first subleading corrections to the index and entropy from the gravity side of the duality. We argue that the corrections to the black hole solution are not needed for the Euclidean on-shell action. It suffices to substitute the leading order solution in the corrected action. We perform this calculation carefully and obtain a precise match with the superconformal index. For the entropy, the corrections to the solution are needed. Here we opt to compute the entropy from the quantum statistical relation and the first law. Finally, we comment on higher-derivative corrections to flavoured theories.

titles.title: Holography and the Quantum Nature of Black Holes

abstracts.value: Quantum networked systems introduce a new class of threats that classical intrusion detection systems (IDS) were not designed to handle, as adversaries can manipulate quantum circuits at the gate, pulse, and measurement levels while also targeting the classical control plane by intercepting encrypted IDS communications for future decryption. This paper addresses this dual threat model by proposing a two-layer defense architecture that jointly secures both the quantum data plane and the IDS infrastructure. The first layer uses machine learning models trained on the Quantum Attack Dataset (QAD) to detect circuit-level attacks under both attack-balanced and heavily skewed class distributions. The second layer protects the IDS control plane with post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) primitives, specifically ML-KEM for key encapsulation and ML-DSA for authentication, mitigating exposure to future decryption attacks. Experimental results across multiple deployment conditions show that tree-based models achieve strong detection performance but degrade under class-prior shift, with pulse-level attacks remaining the most challenging to detect, highlighting limitations of current feature representations. To address this, a confidence-aware policy maps detections to monitoring, verification, and isolation actions, although the verification tier is rarely exercised under the evaluated distributions. The results show that detection and cryptographic protection must be designed together to achieve robust intrusion detection in quantum networked environments.

titles.title: PQC-Secured Intrusion Detection for Quantum Networks: A Two-Layer Defense Architecture

Abstract

The neutron lifetime is an essential parameter in Big Bang nucleosynthesis. It also helps
to determine the element Vud of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix in the
Standard Model of particle physics that represents the up and down quark coupling that
occurs through the weak force. Currently, a 4σ discrepancy exists between beam and trap
lifetime experiments. The Precision Experiment on the Neutron Lifetime Operating with
Proton Extraction (PENeLOPE) is a magneto-gravitational ultracold neutron (UCN) trap
experiment that aims to measure the neutron lifetime with a precision of 0.1 s. Two butterfly
shutters were tested as UCN source and storage valves in PENeLOPEs configuration. Their
average relative leak rates—corrected for background and normalized to the UCN source
transmission rate—were 2.23±1.10 % and 1.01±0.85 %, demonstrating their inadequacy for
the intended purpose. PENeLOPE has stainless steel storage surfaces which can depolarize
UCNs on wall bounce. This affects the systematic uncertainty on the neutron lifetime mea-
surement. Simulations showed the precision goal would be met with a stainless-steel UCN
spin-flip probability (βSS) of 10−5, resulting in a 0.0442 ± 0.0019 s systematic shift of the
neutron lifetime created by marginally trapped UCNs. Fourteen PENeLOPE experiment
runs yielded a statistical precision of 0.0964 ± 0.0012 s, with PENeLOPE installed at the
planned UCN source at Research Neutron Source Heinz Maier-Leibnitz (FRM II) located in
Munich, Germany [1]. Higher βSS values caused prohibitively large systematic shifts, which
could be mitigated by nickel-phosphorous coating to reduce the UCN spin-flip probability
of PENeLOPE’s storage surfaces.

Keywords: Ultracold Neutrons; PENeLOPE; neutron lifetime; UCN

1.1.2 Big Bang Nucleosynthesis

In cosmology, the neutron lifetime influences the abundance ratios of primordial light ele-
ments. Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) is the era when primordial light elements began
to form. At the onset of BBN, the Universe consisted of a hot dense soup of particles inter-
acting with one another in equilibrium. As the Universe expanded, it began to cool down,
corresponding to particles decreasing in kinetic energy energy throughout the Universe from
initially deciseconds to around 200 seconds after the singularity.

Fig. 1.2 shows the ratios of primordial light element abundances as a function of time
and temperature (in units of energy) of the Universe since the big bang up to 106 s after.
The grey dotted line represents the neutron abundance in the Universe that starts at 1 along
with the hydrogen abundance. The ratio of other elements is normalized to the abundance

3



of hydrogen in the Universe. Before 1 s, neutrons and protons were in thermal equilibrium.
The neutron abundance begins to decline as β-decay occurs, then declines more rapidly at
around ∼ 200 s due to the cool down from expansion as nuclei were then able to be formed,
producing light elements such as Helium-4 (Yp), Deuterium and Helium-3. Since β-decay
continually reduces the amount of neutrons in the Universe, the rate of decay, or equivalently
the neutron lifetime τn, affects the abundance of those elements being synthesized.

Since the abundance of primordial elements is dependent on τn, a more precise value of
τn obtained by experiments will constrain the ratio of primordial light element abundances
during BBN.

1.1.3 Beam vs Trap Experiments

Over the last few decades, two methods have been used to determine the lifetime of the free
neutron: beam and trap experiments.

Beam Experiments

Beam experiments measure the number of neutrons in a specific volume from a neutron flux
and detect the decay particles per second in that volume. The rate of neutron decay Ṅ can

4

τn

An example of a typical beam experiment is the National Institute of Standards and

Technology (NIST) neutron lifetime experiment [12], shown in Figure 1.3. A beam of cold
neutrons is sent through a fiducial volume V , where the neutron flux and decay rate are
measured. Downstream, a small percentage of the neutrons are absorbed in a LiF layer
deposited on a silicon substrate. Alphas and tritons emitted from the 6Li +1 n →4 He + t

reaction are detected, and after careful calibration the neutron flux can be deduced. The
protons from β-decay inside the fiducial volume are trapped then detected. From this, the
decay rate Ṅ can be calculated. The challenge with this method is that collection and
detection efficiencies for neutrons, εo, and protons, εp, have to be known to a very high
precision, requiring very careful characterization and calibration of the detectors.

Figure 1.3: NIST neutron lifetime experiment. Cold neutrons and decay protons are mea-

The largest contributions to the precision of the NIST experiment’s neutron lifetime
measurement come from the neutron flux measurement and the detection of α and triton
particle reaction products produced from neutrons interacting with 6Li in the foil. The
detectors measuring the reaction products have their own measurement efficiency εn which
is related to ε0 by

ε0 = εnρfoilσth , (1.6)

section of an incident thermal neutron (neutrons with velocity v = 2000 m/s) interacting
with a 6Li nucleus. The protons from β-decay are trapped for up to 10 ms within a Penning
trap before being adiabatically guided along magnetic field lines towards the proton detector,
which is set on high voltage providing additional acceleration to the protons. The rate of

5

Rp = εpṄ , (1.7)

where εp is the efficiency of the proton decay measurement. The neutron lifetime is then

Trap Experiments

The typical procedure for trap experiments is filling a storage vessel with neutrons, storing
them for a certain amount of time, and then counting them. These experiments use material
walls or magnetic fields along with gravity to contain ultracold neutrons (UCNs)—neutrons
with kinetic energies below 300 neV. A more detailed description of UCNs is provided in
Section 1.2. Stored UCNs that have not decayed during storage are then counted to measure
τn.

The exponential decay function

N(t) = N0e− t

is used to obtain a value of τ by measuring the number of stored UCNs for two different
storage times. N(t) is the number of surviving UCNs in the storage volume at time t, N0 is
the initial stored number of UCNs, and τ is the storage lifetime. Two storage times t1 and
t2 are sufficient to obtain τ by using the exponential decay equation twice

τ = t2 − t1

N2

where N1 and N2 are the number of surviving UCNs measured for the two storage times,
respectively. The relation between τ and τn depends on the neutron loss mechanisms during
storage and the efficiency of neutron detection when neutrons are counted after storage. If
the detection efficiency is different between the two cycles with short and long storage times,
then there will be a systematic effect that comes from a difference in UCN losses between
both cycles. This would cancel if there is no difference in detection efficiency between both
cycles.

6



In UCN trap experiments, accurately determining the initial amount of stored UCNs N0

presents a significant challenge, as it cannot be precisely known. This uncertainty introduces
a limiting factor in achieving precise measurements of the neutron lifetime. To mitigate this
issue, neutron lifetime experiments such as UCNτ at Los Alamos National Laboratory
(LANL) have implemented in situ detection methods, allowing for real-time monitoring of
UCN populations within the trap [13]. This approach enhances the accuracy of neutron
lifetime measurements by reducing uncertainties associated with the initial UCN count.

An example of how the initial stored number of UCNs N0 can change is if a UCN source
for a neutron trap experiment is not stable. This leads to variations in the initial number of
neutrons that fill into the trap N0. If N0 is not consistent between experimental runs, it can
introduce a systematic effect that needs to be corrected. To account for these fluctuations,

The two-storage-time method is a balance between precision and experimental practical-
ity. It allows for accurate determination of the neutron lifetime while minimizing systematic
uncertainties, optimizing resource use, and simplifying data analysis. However, it requires
careful selection of the storage times to ensure that statistical and systematic uncertainties
are minimized.

In an ideal trap, stored neutrons would only be lost due to β-decay leading to τ = τn.
However, trap experiments have more loss channels than just neutron decay that are created
by systematic effects. Stored neutrons may be lost through interactions with the environ-
ment such as absorption or upscattering with the inner surfaces of the storage container or
rest gas. Upscattering in this context refers to low energy neutrons with kinetic energies
less than 300 neV that interact with the trap’s material surface. Through these interactions
these neutrons are sensitive to thermal excitations of the material’s atoms and they can
absorb energy from phonons of the wall material. This energy transfer will then increase
the neutron’s energy over a material trapping energy range and they are then no longer
confined. The absorption interaction will be covered in more detail in Section 1.2. Each of

1.2.1 Strong Force

Fermi was the first to propose that UCNs could completely reflect off material surfaces at any
incident angle [19]. This phenomenon arises from the scattering interaction of an incident
neutron with a collection of nuclei, mediated by the strong nuclear force. The probability
of reflection is determined from the neutron’s wave function. Since the exact potential for
a collection of nuclei is computationally complex and impractical to determine, an effective
potential is employed in the calculation to approximate the neutron wave function. By
using this simplified potential, the Schrödinger equation becomes solvable to obtain an
approximate wavefunction; however, its validity is restricted to low-energy regimes and
regions far from the interaction point [20]. Near the interaction region, the wave function
serves only as an approximation, but it is sufficiently accurate to reproduce key scattering
observables, such as cross-sections.

The theoretical predictions for scattering observables, such as cross-sections and re-
flection probabilities, can be directly compared to experimental results. If the predictions

in reproducing these observables within its validity range.

Spin-flips due to Wall Reflections

When a neutron interacts with a material wall, two types of spin-dependent scattering can
occur: coherent and incoherent scattering. Coherent scattering arises from constructive in-
terference of scattering amplitudes from all nuclei and depends on the average scattering
length, independent of nuclear spin I, reflecting the material’s collective structure. In con-
trast, incoherent scattering stems from variations in individual scattering lengths due to
nuclear spin states or isotopic differences, explicitly depending on the relative spin orien-
tations of the neutron spin Sn and nucleus I. Spin-flip transitions in incoherent scattering
occur through quantum mechanical spin coupling, where three out of four possible spin
configurations of aligned or anti-aligned nuclear spin and neutron spin involve spin flips
(anti-aligned states are related to spin flips), leading to a dominant 2

3 contribution of spin-
flip cross-section to the total incoherent scattering cross-section [24].

15



For characterizing depolarization probability from neutron and material surface interac-
tions, each unique material surface has an associated spin-flip probability per wall bounce
β that is found experimentally. For materials used in UCN experiments, β is typically in
the order of ∼ 10−6 [24, 25]. Experiments that characterize β for different materials can
vary in the strength of the magnetic field used for holding the spin from mT to T ranges of
magnetic field strength.

1.2.4 Weak Force

The weak force is responsible for β-decay as mentioned earlier in Section 1.1. The other forces
that act on UCNs are able to confine or contain them while the weak force is responsible for
their decay process. UCNs with their extremely low kinetic energies, are ideal for precision
studies of the weak interaction due to their ability to be confined in material, magnetic, or
gravitational traps for extended periods.

2.1 Magneto-gravitational trap

The Precision Experiment on the Neutron Lifetime Operating with Proton Extraction (PENe-
LOPE) is a magneto-gravitational trap experiment. PENeLOPE’s objective is to measure
τn with a precision of 0.1 s. The configuration of the experiment is shown in Figure 2.1.
The magnetic field used to store neutrons is created by twenty-four alternating solenoid
coils housing a cylindrical shell storage volume. The coils are made from NbTi wires with
between 32-58 winding layers. The coils are cooled down by a liquid helium cryostat below
the superconducting transition temperature of Tc ∼10 K. The cryostat helium reservoir,
coils and storage volume are protected by a radiation shield surrounding the cylindrical
volume, which is also encased in a vacuum vessel. The inner vertically stacked coils have an
outer radius of around 146 mm and the outer vertically stacked coils have an inner radius
of a little over 500 mm.

There are 11 outer, 9 inner, and 4 bottom cylindrical coils that function to create large
magnetic field gradients at the edge of the UCN storage volume. The nominal current
through the coils produces a magnetic field strength of up to 5.5 T, but the usable field

2.3 Absorber rings

UCNs from the source entering PENeLOPE’s storage volume may have energies above
the magnetic trapping potential. The UCNs that have energies above this potential, but
also have energies below the Fermi potential of the material surfaces, are called marginally
trapped (MT) neutrons because they are not completely contained by the magnetic field
and are able to interact with the storage walls. MT UCNs then have a loss probability per
wall bounce which could reduce the measured storage lifetime measurement τ < τn. In order

21



to minimize the systematic effects that arise from MT UCNs, an absorber is added within
the storage volume in order to reduce the UCN population with total energies higher than
the 115 neV trapping potential. The absorbers will be either titanium which is a neutron
absorber or polyethylene which upscatters neutrons. Both materials have imaginary Fermi
potentials close to or smaller than zero (VTi = −51 neV, VPE = −8.7 neV).

The absorbers shall be in place during the material storage stage of PENeLOPE, when
the main storage magnet is turned off. During the magnetic storage stage, the absorbers
shall be hidden behind the magnetic field for all magnetically trapped neutrons. This only
leaves small spaces of high magnetic field strength close to the storage volume walls. They
are concentric cylindrical shells or rings with a thickness of a few millimeters and are
positioned near the inner and outer surfaces of the storage volume as seen in Fig. 2.1. The
lower edge of the absorbers is situated at a height of about 700 mm from the bottom of the
storage volume to cut off the UCN energy spectrum to ∼80 neV (for the nominal current
of 283.5 A) after filling the storage volume.

During an experiment cycle, the magnetic field will be turned on and off creating a shift
of energy from heating and cooling the polarized UCNs and a cut-off of 80 neV prevents
the heating of UCN above 115 neV. After ramping up the magnetic field, the HFSs that are
constrained to propagate along the material walls undergo many reflections which increases
the probability of spin flips during wall interaction. Since the magnetic field at the walls is
quite large, the HFS might gain a lot of kinetic energy when the spin flips, turning them
into marginally trapped LFS UCN. This can lead to a higher measured storage lifetime.
A side view of HFSs and magnetically trapped LFSs inside PENeLOPE’s storage volume
when the magnetic field is turned on is shown in Figure 2.3. To reduce the HFS population,
the absorber rings will move vertically down along the wall to a position close to the bottom
of the storage volume of ∼5 mm as more HFSs can reach this location. To allow this vertical
movement, actuators will be installed on top of the storage volume attaching to the rings.

2.5 The UCN Source at FRM II

Before moving to TRIUMF in Summer 2024, PENeLOPE was anticipated to be installed
at the Forschungs-Neutronenquelle Heinz Maier-Leibnitz (FRM II) UCN source located
at the Technical University of Munich (TUM). The source operates on the principle of
superthermal UCN production and utilizes a solid deuterium (sD2) converter as its core
technology.

24



Figure 2.5: Schematic representation of the FRM II UCN source. The solid deuterium (sD2)

The UCN source is integrated into the SR6 beamline at FRM II [1]. At its heart is a
toroidal, double-walled aluminum converter vessel, which is maintained at a temperature of
5 K using a supercritical helium cooling loop. To enhance the efficiency of neutron conver-
sion, solid hydrogen (sH2) is used as a premoderator, cooling incoming thermal neutrons
to approximately 40 K before they interact with the sD2 converter. Solid deuterium, frozen
onto the vessels walls by resublimation, facilitates the conversion of thermal neutrons into
UCNs through phonon excitation processes in the crystal lattice.

Thermal neutrons from the reactor, upon entering the sD2 lattice, lose their kinetic en-
ergy through solid-state excitations and are converted into ultracold neutrons with energies
below 230 neV. The produced UCNs are then extracted from the converter and transported
via beamline guides to the experiments. These guides are designed to minimize UCN losses,
with transport efficiencies of 99% per meter for neutrons in the energy range of 100–200 neV.

The source is currently in the non-nuclear testing stage before installing and commis-
sioning at FRM II. It is expected to deliver a flux density of 6×105 UCN/cm2/s at the SR6

FRM II UCN source in Chapter 4.

2.6 PENeLOPE Experiment Cycle

PENeLOPE’s foreseen experiment cycle is similar to all bottle experiments with the trap
method, which includes filling, storing, and counting. However, more stages are included:
two ramping stages for turning the magnetic field on or off, and two stages for cleaning out
unwanted UCN from the storage volume. PENeLOPE’s experiment cycle consists of seven
stages in total. Approximate stage durations are given in brackets.

1. Filling (∼200 s): UCNs are transported from a source to PENeLOPE’s storage volume.

2. Marginally-trapped (MT) cleaning (∼200 s): The storage valve is closed. UCNs in the
storage volume with energies above the magnetic trapping potential are removed by
absorber rings placed at a certain height within the trap.

3. Ramp-up (100 s): The coil current is increased to the nominal current which produces
the magnetic trapping potential.

4. High-field Seeker Cleaning (∼60 s): HFSs populate the region close to the storage
walls. They are cleaned out through an absorber moving from top to bottom near the
inner and outer surfaces of the storage volume.

5. Storage (∼20-1550 s): UCNs are stored within the storage volume for two predefined
durations (t1 and t2) to calculate τ with a short and long storage time. The proton
detector counts the decay protons that are produced only during this stage.

6. Ramp-down (100 s): The magnetic field is turned off over a span of 100 s for trapped
UCN to exit the storage volume for counting.

7. Counting (∼300 s): UCN are given time to reach the detector after exiting the storage
volume.

Certain components are moved or turned on during different stages such as the UCN
Switch flap. Table 2.1 shows the component configuration in each stage. The UCN switch
flap has three positions: The filling position allows UCN to propagate to the storage volume
closing off their path to the UCN detector, the middle position opens the path from both
the UCN source volume and to the UCN detector, and the detector position allows UCN to
propagate from the storage volume to the UCN detector blocking off the path to the UCN
source. The next subsections contain a detailed description of all cycles.

2.6.1 Filling

The filling stage is the first stage in the experiment cycle during which UCNs are transported
from the anticipated UCN source at the FRM II into PENeLOPE’s storage volume. The
energy spectrum of the source plays a significant role, since PENeLOPE should be placed
at a height, where the maximum of the spectrum can be magnetically stored inside the
experiment, balanced by gravity. Guides that have VF > En are used to propagate UCNs
into the storage volume. The source and storage valves are open and the UCN switch directs
UCNs from the source to the storage volume. The UCNs are polarized after entering the
guide from the source before reaching the switch. A spin holding field, created by a current
flowing through the central rod, maintains UCN polarization once they enter into the storage
volume. The magnetic field created by the superconducting magnet to store UCNs is not on
at this time, so UCNs in the storage volume will interact with the inner and outer surface
walls of the storage volume.

2.6.2 Marginally Trapped UCN Cleaning

After the filling stage, the storage valve is closed and marginally trapped UCNs—those
with total energies exceeding the equipotential limit of ∼115 neV (only at nominal current)
imposed by the magneto-gravitational field—are removed. The UCN switch flap is then ro-
tated into the middle position to dump the remaining UCNs in the guides into the detector.
The absorber rings, placed at 700 mm above the bottom of the storage volume, remove
these UCNs leaving the UCNs in the storage volume with maximum total energies under
∼80 neV. The reason for setting the absorbers at that specific height will be explained in
section 2.6.3. The absorbers’ positions may be changed to cut off the energy spectrum at
other energies if needed. In the current configuration, the absorber is kept at a height of
∼700 mm above the bottom of the storage volume from the start of filling and continuing
until a certain cleaning time to sufficiently clean the MT UCN population.

27



2.6.3 Magnetic Field Ramp-up

At the beginning of the ramp-up stage, the UCN switch flap remains in its position to
open the path between the storage volume and the UCN detector. Since the storage valve
remains closed, the UCN detected at this point would be any that come from leaks through
the valves or background. A magnetic field is introduced by increasing the current through
the superconducting coils. The magnetic field increases over a span of 100 s until the nominal
current is reached. As the magnetic field strength increases, the total energy of UCNs is
altered due to the time-varying magnetic potential. This potential acts as a dynamic barrier,
effectively behaving as a moving mirror in the reference frame of the UCNs. Depending on
the phase of interaction, UCNs reflecting off this moving potential experience a change in
momentum, leading to either a gain or loss of kinetic energy. LFSs are heated or gain total
energy while the HFSs are cooled or lose total energy. By the end of this stage the LFSs
with total energies under 115 neV are completely trapped within the equipotential lines as
shown on the left side of Fig. 2.2. LFSs with higher total energies that are not completely
trapped within the equipotential lines are considered MT UCNs that still interact with
the material walls. The HFS population is attracted to regions close to the material walls
subjecting the HFS population to have more losses than the LFS population through wall
interactions.

2.6.4 High-field Seeker Cleaning

Once the magnetic field reaches its maximum value, the HFSs are removed via absorbers.
They are not trapped by the magneto-gravitational field within the storage volume at any
total energy. The absorber rings remove the HFSs by lowering down from their height of
∼700 mm to ∼5 mm above the bottom of the storage volume and are held there for roughly
20 s until they are brought back up to 700 mm. The storage valve is opened at the start of
this stage to release any marginally trapped UCNs or HFSs into the detector, serving both
to remove these unwanted UCNs and to provide a comparative measurement between runs.
The fully trapped LFSs are contained by the magnetic field and gravity so they should only
experience losses through β−decay during this stage even with the absorbers moving up
and down as long as it does not cross the 115 neV equipotential line. The proton detector
is activated during this stage to provide insight on how the population changes.

2.6.5 Storage

The storage stage starts after the HFS cleaning stage with a majority of fully trapped LFSs
plus a smaller fraction of the partially trapped MT UCNs and/or HFSs within the storage
volume. The absorbers stay at 700 mm, the magnetic field is held constant, the storage valve
stays open, and the UCN switch connects the storage volume to the UCN detector. The
proton detector is operational during the entirety of this stage to detect the decay protons

28



from UCN β−decay. For a full experiment cycle, the storage durations are t1 = 20 s and
t2 = 1550 s for this study, similar to the UCNτ experiment [13]. Systematic effects arise
from losses of marginally trapped UCNs and high-field seekers within the storage volume
during this stage.

2.6.6 Magnetic Field Ramp-down

After storage the remaining surviving UCN need to be counted in the UCN detector which
requires the magnetic field to be turned off. The UCN switch, storage valve, and absorber
remain in the same position as during the storage stage. The magnetic field is then decreased
slowly over 100 s until completely off. The detection of UCN starts during this stage. As the
magneto-gravitational equipotential barrier decreases, all UCNs, including those previously
trapped magnetically, are able to exit the storage volume and are guided to the UCN
detector.

2.6.7 Counting

Once the magnetic field is turned off, the remaining UCN within the storage volume are
given time to reach the detector. During this stage, the UCN switch, storage valve, and
absorber are in the same configuration as the previous stage. At this point, no distinction
between HFSs and LFSs is made since the detection is not spin sensitive. The final UCN
count is then acquired from the portion of UCN that were able to be detected. N1 and N2

from Eq. 1.10 are determined from the background corrected integral of UCN counts during
the ramp-down and counting stage for t1 and t2, respectively. The losses of UCN along the
way to the detector is modeled by a collection efficiency through simulations.

Three components at Technische Universität München (TUM) were available as viable can-

detector: a replica UCN guide, and two butterfly shutters. It was necessary to characterize

the storage lifetime in the replica guide and the leak rates of the butterfly shutters. These
experiments were conducted at the TRIGA (Training Research Isotope production Gen-

3.1 UCN Transport Components

UCN storage experiment cycles typically start with neutrons being transported from a
source to a storage volume. UCN transport components must be enclosed, such as cylindrical
guides with surface Fermi potential values large enough to allow UCNs to propagate while
reflecting off their inner surfaces. The enclosed volume must also have a suitable vacuum for
neutrons to have a low enough probability of being absorbed by rest gas. The reflectivity
of the guides plays a crucial role in the UCN transport efficiency, with surface roughness
being a key factor. Rough surfaces result in non-specular reflections, where neutrons scatter
in random directions rather than reflecting uniformly, causing a diffusive transport process.
This increases the number of reflections required for a neutron to travel a specific distance,
unlike smooth surfaces that enable specular reflection, thereby significantly reducing the
transmission efficiency of the guide. To address these challenges, extensive research and
development efforts are underway at various laboratories to enhance the properties of UCN
guides [26].

One method to achieve a guide with a smooth surface and high Fermi potential involves
replicating the glass-like smoothness onto nickel composites to fabricate replica guides. By

3.1.1 Replica Guide

Replica guides, as shown in Fig. 3.1, have been shown to have good UCN transport charac-
teristics [26]. They are a viable option for PENeLOPE. They are produced by the company
Sputter-Dünnschichttechnik Heidelberg (SD-H). They are made of a nickel-vanadium (NiV)
thin film alloy composition consisting of 93% nickel and 7% vanadium. To produce a replica
guide, a thin film is sputtered onto glass to a thickness of ∼100 nm and then a backing
composition of pure nickel is used to support the film resulting in a combined thickness
of 0.5 mm [27]. The alloy is then peeled off the glass and rolled. The backing is welded
along the rolled alloy’s length to form a cylinder with an inner diameter of 115 mm. This
thin-walled tube is not able to sustain a pressure difference of 1 bar so it is necessary to
enclose it within a stainless steel vacuum enclosure. The guides have a Fermi potential of
∼252 neV. Their surface roughness of under 10 Å[26] is equivalent to the roughness of the
original glass as it was copied from the sputtering. UCNs that propagate through the guide
still have a probability of being absorbed or upscattered with each wall interaction. During
the characterization experiment in Mainz, four 0.5 m replica guides were installed in series
to form a 2 m long storage volume.

3.2.1 TRIGA Reactor and UCN Source

The TRIGA reactor at Mainz offers two modes of operation, the first being a steady
state mode or continuous operation at 100 kW that provides a thermal neutron flux of
1012 n/(cm2 s). The other is a pulse mode which increases the instantaneous neutron flux
up to 250 MW within a 30 ms window 12 times per hour. The peak flux of neutrons is
up to 2 × 1015 n/cm2 s. The reactor core fuel elements have a chemical composition of
Uranium(20 % 235U)-Zirconiumhydride(UZrH) [28]. The hydrogen acts as a moderator,
providing inherent safety if the fuel elements increase in temperature. The neutrons pro-
duced during the heating will increase in energy, resulting in lower fission reaction rates until
fission is stopped completely. Figure 3.3 shows a horizontal cross-section of the reactor core
with beamports to guide neutrons out from the core. UCNs are produced at beamports C
and D. Beamport C was used for the PENeLOPE component characterization experiments.

Beamport C uses solid deuterium to convert thermal neutrons into ultracold neutrons.

3.2.4 UCN detector

The detector used in these experiments is a cascade UCN detector [31]. The cascade detector
is able to detect a UCN flux on the order of 107n/cm2s. It has an Al foil entrance window
with a Fermi potential of 54 neV and a thickness of 100 µm. Neutrons that pass through
the window interact with a 10B layer coated on a drift electrode leading to the reactions

10B + n −→ 7Li + α + 2.79 MeV (6%), (3.2)

and
10B + n −→ 7Li + α + 2.31 MeV (94%). (3.3)

The products from these reactions then ionize atoms in a gas mixture inside of the reaction
chamber, typically argon and carbon dioxide, ArCO2. The ionized atoms then interact with
gas electron multiplier (GEM) foils creating electrons. These electrons are then amplified
by being accelerating through an electric field in the holes between the GEM foils. The
amplified electrons then drift to a printed circuit board (PCB) readout. The PCB readout
is a key part of the electronic system, designed to capture, amplify, and transmit data about
neutron interactions occurring in the detector.

3.2.6 Filling Time Optimization

The optimum filling time was found by measuring the saturation curve shown in Figure 3.13
of neutrons filled into the storage volume and then immediately emptied into the detector.
Neutron counts were recorded for various filling times {0 s, 4 s, 6 s, 8 s, 10 s, 20 s, 30 s,

randomized order of 23 runs and were plotted by averaging neutron counts obtained for
each predetermined filling time. The durations of the other stages were held constant for
each run: tstore = 10 s, tcounting = 80 s, and ttransmission = 50 s. tfill = 20 s was chosen as a
compromise between reaching saturation in the number of neutrons stored and saving time

The BS1 and BS2 shutter leak experiments were conducted separately with the same set

3.2.9 Storage Lifetime Experiment Analysis & Results

The storage lifetime is determined by filling neutrons into a trap, holding them for varying
storage times tstore and counting the surviving neutrons in a detector. The experiment was
conducted on two different days, designated Day 1 and Day 2.

Other measurements include background (BG) counts and BS1 UCN leak counts. BG
counts may come from different sources such as electronic BG that is always there, a cold
and faster neutron BG that come from when the reactor and UCN source are operational,
and a BG due to leaks through valves which is present when the reactor and UCN source are
operational but suppressed when more than 1 valve is closed. The cold and faster neutron
BG differs from the BG due to leaks through valves because cold neutrons do not have the

44



same property as UCNs of being totally reflected at any incident angle off a surface, so cold
and faster neutrons have a chance to interact with the guide surfaces but are not contained
like UCNs. The best period for background determination is the storage period, where both
shutters BS1 and BS2 were closed as seen in Fig. 3.10. The BG measured during the storage
period takes into consideration all the possible BGs that were mentioned above. These BG
measurements during storage are used to find an overall BG which includes a count from the
UCN leak through BS2 measured as well during the storage stage. The BS1 and BS2 leaks
affect the overall detected population. The BS1 leak during the storage period is illustrated
in Fig. 3.10. UCNs can propagate through a closed BS1 from both directions from the source
to the storage volume or from the storage volume to the source. The effect of UCNs leaving
the storage volume through BS leaks influences the measurement of τst. The incoming UCNs
from the source that leak into the storage volume provide a net positive effect since UCN
density will be higher upstream of BS1 compared to downstream (storage volume), so the
BS1 leak into the storage volume is constant since the source provides a constant flux. This
complicates the τst calculation through having a N(tstore) measurement that includes these
UCN gains and losses during storage.

PENeLOPE

Chapter Summary

This chapter focuses on analyzing three critical factors to determine whether the measure-
ment of the neutron lifetime using PENeLOPE can achieve the target precision of 0.1 s.
The following factors are examined:

1. Systematic Effects and Marginally Trapped (MT) UCN: Some UCNs are not
fully trappable within PENeLOPE, leading to systematic shifts in the measured neutron
lifetime. Of particular focus in this work is the contribution of marginally trapped (MT)
UCNs with total energies exceeding the magneto-gravitational trapping potential of 115 neV.
These neutrons may be lost during storage and cause shifts in the neutron lifetime mea-
surement. To address this issue, the duration of the MT cleaning stage, described in Section
2.6, is optimized to reduce the MT UCN population and minimize its impact on the mea-
surement.

2. Spin-Flip Probability of Stainless Steel: The walls of PENeLOPE’s storage volume
are composed of stainless steel, and UCN interactions with the storage walls can cause neu-
tron spin flips. This affects the ratio of low-field seekers to high-field seekers in PENeLOPE.
The spin-flip probability per wall bounce of stainless steel (βSS) is not well known. Only one
published result of βSS = 3.36 × 10−3 can be found and only in a conference presentation
that was not peer reviewed [24, 38]. This value is more than two orders of magnitude higher
than other β values for typical UCN component materials listed in Table 4.2. Due to the
potential uncertainty in this measurement, a parameter sweep of βSS with three values of
2 × 10−3, 10−4 and 10−5 was performed. A higher spin flip probability affects the viability
of PENeLOPE dramatically as will be shown in Section 4.3.3.

3. Number of Cycles Needed to Achieve a Statistical Precsion of 0.1 s: Section
4.3.4 presents the number of experimental cycles necessary to reach a statistical precision of

53



0.1 s on the neutron lifetime assuming PENeLOPE is operated at the planned UCN source
at the FRM II.

Methodology Employed

The method for analyzing the precision of the neutron lifetime measured using PENeLOPE
involves several steps. To start, simulations of UCNs in PENeLOPE are performed using
the PENTrack program, described in the next Section 4.1, to emulate full PENeLOPE
experiment cycles. Each of the seven stages of the experiment cycle, described in Section
2.6, are simulated independently. This is necessary since the stage durations need to be
varied to achieve an optimal compromise between statistical sensitivity and systematic
effects. To this end, the neutron population in PENeLOPE is divided up into 5 neV energy
bins and into low-field seekers (LFSs) and high-field seekers (HFSs). The assumption here
is that UCNs are characterized sufficiently by sorting them into a specific energy and spin
orientation bin. This is valid since the nature of diffuse wall reflections randomized neutron
trajectories efficiently so that the phase space of neutrons is in equilibrium. In practical
terms, this means that any neutron in a particular bin, no matter its location and velocity
vector has an almost equal probability of reaching any other accessible location in the
experiment. To properly connect one experimental stage to the next, a survival probability
is calculated for each energy bin which is used to evolve the energy distribution for LFSs and
HFSs through all seven stages. These distributions are created at each full second during
the whole experiment and all stage durations can be varied with this granularity without
requiring to run new simulations.

Furthermore, various combinations of stage durations can be chosen to make many ex-
periment cycles. This work focuses on varying one particular stage duration, the MT clean-
ing stage. All other stage durations are kept constant and set close to recommendations from
a previous publication [2]. Table 4.1 shows simulated stage durations that were arbitrarily
chosen and optimum durations that were chosen to simplify and reduce the optimization
routine to just varying the MT cleaning stage time.

To measure the exponential time constant of the neutron beta decay, two durations have
to be chosen for the magnetic storage period from Eq. 1.10. 20 s and 1550 s were adopted
following [13].

Simulation Stages and Key Analyses

UCN energy distribution histograms for both high-field seeking and low-field seeking neu-
trons from simulations were used to track UCNs through a PENeLOPE experiment cycle.
In the following, I provide a summary of the main objectives of each simulated stage as I
discuss them in Section 4.2.1 in further detail.
1. Filling Stage

• Objective: Normalize energy distributions of LFSs and HFSs based on the UCN
source flux at FRM II. The source fills neutrons into the storage volume of PENe-
LOPE. Pre-polarization is done between source and storage volume to reduce the
number of HFSs in PENeLOPE during filling.

• Stage is used to explain: LFS energy distributions are used to explain the nor-
malization process, which involves scaling the simulated production rate to the UCN
source flux using Equation 4.8. Although not shown, HFS distributions are normalized
through the same process.

2. Marginally Trapped (MT) Cleaning

• Objective: Remove UCNs from the storage volume that cannot be fully magnetically
stored, and which are prone to losses due to wall interactions.

• Stage is used to explain: The energy distributions of subsequent stages must be
connected to the filling stage, maintaining normalization relative to the UCN source, to
accurately track UCNs through the energy distributions across an entire PENeLOPE
cycle. As the spectrum progresses, it evolves due to effects introduced at each stage.

55



To account for this, the connection is established by calculating survival probability
distributions for each stage, which are then adjusted—both scaled and shaped—using
the experiment distribution from the preceding stage.

• Main Observations: Higher energy UCNs are effectively removed if the spin flip
probability of the storage walls is low enough.

3. Ramp-up Stage

• Objective: Turn on main magnetic field to transition from material storage in PENe-
LOPE to magnetic storage.

• Stage is used to explain: The LFS and HFS energy shift distributions are used to
observe the shifts caused by the magnetic field. Simulations that start with only LFSs
or only HFSs are created for all stages with a magnetic field to separate spin-flipped
UCN into additional energy distributions. This distinction ensures a comprehensive
understanding of how the magnetic field influences energy dynamics.

• Main Observations: High-field seekers lose energy, low-field seekers gain energy.

4. HFS Cleaning (Stages A & B)

• Objective: Remove HFSs via lowering of absorber rings.

• Stage is used to explain: HFS energy distributions are plotted to visualize the
removal of HFSs using absorber rings. Special attention is given to empty bins in
the energy distribution, as low statistics may lead to inaccuracies. Another approach
estimates the experimental distributions for these stages by utilizing calculated storage
lifetimes to determine the distributions.

Since the simulations with the magnetic field turned on start with either HFSs or
LFSs, this allows for observations on the impact of first-order spin flips to second-
order spin flips on the ratio of HFSs to LFSs stored in PENeLOPE. The production
of HFSs from spinflips is estimated for each simulation with different βSS.

5. Storage Stage

• Objective: To store LFSs with total energies under the magneto-gravitational po-
tential 115 neV for a short storage time of t1 = 20 s and a long storage time of
t2 = 1550 s.

• Stage is used to explain: The analysis focuses on the impact of marginally trapped
UCNs (MT UCNs) during this stage, evaluating how their losses during wall interac-
tions affect the neutron lifetime. However, the inclusion of β-decay in the simulations
introduces significant uncertainties, primarily due to low statistics. These uncertain-
ties could overshadow the effect of MT UCN losses on the neutron lifetime, making

56



it challenging to isolate and accurately assess their specific contribution. To get past
this issue, a filtering process is applied to exclude UCNs that undergo β−decay in the
simulations. This way, LFS energy distributions would only be dependent on other
loss mechanisms other than β−decay.

• Main Observations: UCN losses that occur during this stage contribute to a shift
of the measured neutron lifetime. Energy distributions are dependent on the value of
βSS . Low statistics in simulations makes β−decay have a high statistical uncertainty.

6. Ramp-Down and Counting Stage

• Objective: Magnetic field is turned off, LFSs and HFSs are counted.

• Stage is used to explain: The β−decay filtering applied in the storage stage is
corrected to account for the decay effects in the final combined energy distribution.
The ramp-down and counting stage’s energy distribution is connected with the storage
stage to obtain the final experiment distribution at the end of the PENeLOPE cycle.
The connection is done by applying the effect of this stage to the storage stage’s
experiment distribution. The collection efficiency is calculated for simulations with
each βSS .

4.1.2 PENTrack Inputs and Outputs

PENTrack has the option to accept computer-aided design (CAD) models in stereolitho-
graphic (STL) format to simplify the implementation of complex experiment geometries.
Each component of the CAD model is assigned material properties relevant for UCN inter-
action such as the scattering parameters, Fermi potentials VF and WF and the probability
of spin flip on wall bounce β. Material inputs for selected materials used in PENTrack
simulations for this study are shown in Table 4.2. Every component may be assigned user-
defined inactive times that allow them to appear or disappear at specified times during
the simulation. This is used to mimic moving parts, such as valves or switches, by copying
a component into different positions and changing their active times. Moving geometries
are not supported in PENTrack, yet. A simplified PENeLOPE CAD model used in these
simulations is shown in Figure 4.2.

59



The UCN switch has a flap inside that can be moved into three positions as described in
Section 2.4. To model this movement in PENTrack, because moving parts are not supported,
the flap is copied into the three positions and inactive times are assigned that would omit
these positions of the flap from the model at appropriate times. The storage valve is modeled
as a completely tight flat plate blocking the whole UCN entrance guide to PENeLOPE when
it is active. The absorber rings on the inside and outside walls of the PENeLOPE storage
volume, described in Section 2.3, are 10 cm high and protrude 5 mm into the storage volume
from the walls. Three possible positions are implemented depending on which absorber rings
are active or inactive.

Aside from material properties and changing inactive/active times of geometries used in
PENTrack, more user-defined inputs for UCN initial conditions such as maximum simulation
time, initial polarization, etc. are set up in a configuration file. Examples of these input
files are in Section A.1. Selected input parameters are seen in Table 4.3. In this research,
neutrons were the only particles simulated, while their decay products were excluded from
consideration. The simulated particles’ initial kinetic energy range along with an energy
spectrum function are also input parameters that are user-defined which may be utilized
to mimic a specific UCN source. In this work, the energy spectrum obtained from previous
simulations for the planned UCN source at FRM II is utilized [44]. The UCN source at FRM
II is described in Section 2.5. A magnetic field map may be used via table files created by
finite element software. A 2D, rotationally symmetric field map of the superconducting
magnet of PENeLOPE was created through the Opera3D software produced by Dassault
Systemes [45] in a previous study [37]. Additionally, a vertical current-carrying rod of 12.5 kV
in the center of PENeLOPE creates the spin holding field as described in Section 2.1. This
is represented by a line current in PENTrack and computed using the Biot-Savart law.

PENTrack records particle characteristics that are user-specified for the start and end
of a particle trajectory, such as initial and final simulation time t, Cartesian coordinates
(x, y, z), total energies H, and polarization p. They are saved in what will be referred to as
an end log file. This file can be saved as a ROOT [46] file which reorganizes the recorded
values into a data tree structure for analysis with ROOT or pyROOT. Other values that
may be recorded in the end log are: the number of times a particle hits a surface, Nhit, the
number of spin-flips per wall reflection, Nspinflip, and material number where the neutron
stopped being tracked, solidend.

PENTrack can also record the properties of the simulated particles at selected times
during the simulation in what are called snapshot log files. Similarly to the end log files,
the user inputs which properties are to be saved into the snapshot log files. The difference
between the snapshot and end log files is that the particle properties are recorded at user-
specified times during the simulation instead of at the end of a particle track. One can
use the snapshot logs to examine the neutron behavior throughout the simulation such as
particle trajectory. In this study, snapshots are saved every second.

4.1.3 Simulation Limitations

Before discussing the processes and effects in each stage of PENeLOPE’s experimental cycle
through simulations performed in this study, it is important to address the limitations in
statistics that became a bottleneck in the studies of PENeLOPE using simulations.

In PENTrack, only one particle is simulated at a time. The precision on the neutron
lifetime measurement using trap experiments depends heavily on the number of UCNs that
can be stored in the trap’s storage volume. From the results presented in Section 4.2.1, it
has been established that PENeLOPE is capable of storing approximately 107 UCNs in a
single run after filling from an operational UCN source at the FRM II. To reduce statistical
uncertainty, multiple runs must be performed to increase the total number of UCNs stored
and detected. The required number of runs was found to be 14 from the analysis in Section
4.3.4. This means that more than 108 UCNs would need to be simulated to achieve full
statistical precision.

When simulations of UCNs in PENeLOPE were first undertaken, the time required to
simulate full statistics was underestimated. To address the limitation of PENTrack simu-
lating only one particle at a time, the Cedar computing cluster from the Digital Research
Alliance of Canada [47] was utilized to execute PENTrack simulations on multiple CPUs in
parallel. By simulating each stage separately, it was found that the storage stage demanded
the most computational resources. This was due to the 2000 s duration of the storage simu-
lation, which is at least four times longer than other stages, and the magnetic field applied
during this stage. The magnetic field introduces additional computational complexity by
requiring more integration steps to process UCN trajectories along magnetic field lines,
thereby increasing the time per simulation.

Using PENTrack on Cedar [47], approximately 106 UCNs were simulated during the
storage stage by partitioning the workload into smaller tasks. Each PENTrack run was
configured to simulate 120 UCNs, and 10 jobs were submitted simultaneously. Each job
consisted of 1000 tasks, with each task running on a single CPU, allowing 1000 CPUs to be
used concurrently. This configuration enabled the simulation of 120,000 UCNs per job. By
repeating this process across multiple jobs, 106 UCNs were achieved, but this was still several
orders of magnitude below the required statistics. Simulating these 106 UCNs consumed
roughly 75,000 CPU hours. Extrapolating to full statistics would require approximately
7.5 × 106 CPU hours, or about 313 days on Cedar.

Achieving full statistics was further complicated by the intent to simulate different mate-
rial properties, such as varying the spin-flip probability βSS of stainless steel on PENeLOPEs
storage surfaces. Each βSS value increased the total simulation time by a factor of three due
to the need to simulate multiple configurations of PENeLOPE.

62



Given the unrealistic timeframe required to achieve full statistics, the analysis was com-
pleted by rescaling results from the lower-statistics simulations, accounting for the higher
statistical uncertainties that arise from this approach.

4.2 Simulating a PENeLOPE Cycle using PENTrack

PENTrack has the ability to simulate a full PENeLOPE run cycle in one simulation by
changing the input parameters to follow each of the seven stage configurations. Attempting
to simulate a full PENeLOPE run for each combination of stage durations would be ex-
ceedingly computationally costly in both time and storage. To avoid this bottleneck, each
stage in the PENeLOPE cycle is simulated separately. These stage simulations are then
connected to complete a run cycle through probability distribution histograms of UCN en-
ergy which are recorded each second during each stage. This process is described in more
detail in Sections 4.2.2 and 4.2.3.

The analysis is performed by storing the UCN population within PENeLOPE’s storage
volume into histograms of UCN total energy H using 5 neV bins between −200 and 300 neV
as seen in Figure 4.4. The initial and final total energies Hstart and Hend are defined to be the
sum of the kinetic and potential energies without the rest mass energy of the UCNs. Both,
high-field seekers and low-field seekers are recorded. Figures of LFS energy distributions
from simulations with βSS = 2 × 10−3 are used to describe UCNs in the filling and MT
cleaning stage simulations.

Phase Space Weighting

A UCN population within a material trap can be modeled as a classical gas capable of
achieving a quasi-statistical equilibrium known as mechanical equilibrium. UCN popula-
tions in mechanical equilibrium are characterized by isotropy of the gas in momentum
space [19]. Since UCNs have a chance to reflect off of material walls in a non-specular fash-
ion, the momentum vectors of stored UCNs will be uniformly distributed in all directions
after many wall bounces. The momentum phase space available for a given UCN density
is energy dependent, so gravity, magnetic fields, and Fermi potentials change the accessible
phase space of the UCN gas. For example, if the UCN gas is in a gravitational field, the

67



available phase space contracts with height. To simulate neutrons starting within PENe-
LOPE’s storage volume, the available phase space must be considered to determine their
initial positions, ensuring a more realistic simulation. In PENTrack, implementing phase
space weighting requires specifying a source volume geometry. This geometry defines the
region where neutrons originate and serves as the basis for initializing the phase space
weighting process.

PENTrack simulates a neutron by first choosing a random initial position within the
source volume geometry, with an initial kinetic energy sampled from a predefined distribu-
tion. When phase space weighting is active, a minimum potential energy Vmin of the system
is found by randomly selecting many spatial points inside the volume and overwriting Vmin

if Vnew < Vmin. Rejection sampling is then done by sampling particles with various starting
times and positions which are only simulated through being accepted by a probability of
